series.title: Reading The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas
series.deck: Two essays on a door beneath the summer festival and the road out of the city. How does Omelas learn to keep that door shut? What can the people who walk away decide for anyone but themselves?
series.source_note: Ursula K. Le Guin’s 1973 short story. Full spoilers.

ui.series: Reading The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas

articles.title: The Door Beneath the Festival
body: The horse race hasn't started yet. At the edge of the crowd, a child of nine or ten is playing a wooden flute alone. People stop to listen and smile, but no one interrupts. When the child lowers the flute, a trumpet sounds by the starting line.

Le Guin lets us linger in places like this. What sort of trains should Omelas have? Should there be beer? The narrator is happy to let us decide. She doesn't want us to take the people of Omelas for fools just because they're happy. As the summer festival gets underway, she asks if we believe in it. If we still don't, she has one more thing to tell us.

Somewhere in the city there's a small room with no window. It may be beneath a handsome public building, or it may be in somebody's cellar. The child in the room looks six but is nearly ten, about the age of the flute player. The door is usually locked, but it opens now and then. Some people hurry to put down food and water; some stand in the doorway and look. The child still remembers sunlight and the sound of its mother's voice, and sometimes begs whoever comes to let it out. No one at the door ever answers.

Everyone in the city knows about the room, though not everyone has seen it. Children usually hear about it between the ages of eight and twelve. Some who go to see the child come home in tears. Others are too angry to speak. The terms they are given are clear: if the child were brought out into the sun, washed, fed and comforted, the prosperity and joy Omelas now enjoys would vanish. There is one more rule: no one may speak so much as a kind word to the child.

For some people it takes weeks, for others years, to come around to the thought that the child would probably be little better off outside. After being afraid for so long, the child might even find sunlight painful. In time, those walls and that darkness can start to look like protection.

Something has changed. At first, what people couldn't bear was that the child was locked in there. Now the harm done by keeping the child there so long is what persuades them to keep the door shut. The child may really be afraid of the light. It may take a long time before someone can come near without frightening the child. Those are things to think about when caring for the child. But the people of Omelas have thought further ahead on the child's behalf: without ever letting the child out, they say there would be little to gain from freedom.

Later the story brings us back to the wooden flute. People in the city believe that if the child below weren't there suffering, the child above couldn't play such a happy tune. The narrator even says that knowing what happens in that room makes them gentle with children. The flute player doesn't need to know anyone is listening. Elsewhere in the city, a child knows there are people in the doorway and has asked them to be let out. The people who heard put down food and water and shut the door again.
articles.deck: One child plays a wooden flute by the crowd. Another, about the same age, asks to be let out. How does Omelas learn to keep the door shut?

articles.title: The Road Out of Omelas
body: Sometimes a young person who has seen the child doesn't go home. There are older people, too, who fall silent for a day or two and then go out. They walk alone, each through the city gates and on across the fields. After dark there are still villages to pass, with lights in the windows. They go west or north, toward the mountains, and do not come back.

The people who stay aren't necessarily indifferent. Those who have seen the child really are angry, and really do feel powerless. Le Guin has given them a hard enough choice. Even if we take the story on its own terms and grant that letting the child out would cost the city the happiness it has now, one thing is still unsettled: if everyone in Omelas depends on that room, does that give them the right to keep a child locked inside?

The story never has the door open because someone walks away. Those who leave can decide not to stay here any longer. The child behind the door has no such road. Keeping the two things apart means we don't have to call leaving a rescue, or say that leaving makes no difference simply because it doesn't rescue the child. What the people who leave refuse is their own part in what happens here. The child is still in the room.

Reading this, I also think about what it would mean to stay and open the door. Someone who stays can talk to others, can go to the door. But opening it needn't be the end of the work. A child who fears the light could stay somewhere dim at first, with food to eat and someone to look after them. When the child wants to go farther, they can. The people of Omelas needn't decide in advance what sort of life the child ought to have outside.

Those are the questions the story leaves me with. Le Guin's last scene is still outside the city. The narrator can't say what the place is like or even be sure there is such a place. Those who walk away seem to know where they're going. The last we see of them, they're walking toward the mountains. If the child behind the door could walk out too, we could wait for the child to say which way they want to go.
articles.deck: Those who leave can choose their own road. The child behind the door has no road out, and opening the door would only be a beginning.
